transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-03-21
- Start: 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~54 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Elena Morris (Stratagem Head of Data), Jon Park (Platform Eng), Priya Singh (CTO)

Summary: cost-econ deep dive; trying to size hosted vs dedicated; understand batching, KV/prefix caching, quantization tradeoffs, and pilot next steps.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um this is Maya from Redwood. we have Ravi, our SE, on the line too. how's everyone doing?
[00:06] Elena: Good thanks, excited to dig in, we've been looking at reducing spend on generation for our analyst tools.
[00:10] Priya: Hi all. quick note, we care a lot about budget predictability and also some data stays on prem, but much can be hosted.
[00:18] Ravi: great, so high level we want to surface the levers: per-token pricing (hosted), reserved/dedicated capacity commits, and engineering levers like batching, prefix/KV cache and quantization. we'll also talk about typical pilot steps and what numbers you should share.
[00:30] Jon: quick context — right now we run ~100M generation tokens/month on a mix of public APIs, bursty traffic, 3-4k concurrent users but most are interactive queries ~1-2 per user per minute. current spend is about $22k/mo and it's spiking.
[00:45] Maya: ok so your target is around $15k/mo long term?
[00:48] Priya: yeah that's the engineering target; business might expand but initial constraint is 15k.
[00:52] Ravi: good. rough math — hosted per-token pricing varies by model, but you can get to cheaper unit economics by (1) batching requests to increase tokens per kernel call, (2) enabling KV/prefix caching for repeated context, (3) quantized model variants for inference. with dedicated, you trade upfront commit for much lower per-token GPU marginal cost.
[01:10] Elena: can you show a concrete example?
[01:14] Ravi: sure. imagine 1B tokens/month. on hosted for an Llama-style 13B model, ballpark is X cents per 1k tokens, but with caching and batching you might reduce perceived cost per effective token by 20-40%. with dedicated, if you reserve a pool of GPUs you end up with fixed monthly capacity cost — so if you fully utilize it measured as tokens/sec and batch size, the per-token goes down substantially, often 2-5x better on highly utilized steady workloads.
[01:36] Jon: we are not at 1B, more like 100-200M range to start. does dedicated still make sense?
[01:42] Ravi: it depends on utilization. if you can get steady utilization above ~40-50% of a dedicated pool, dedicated can be cost effective even at 200M tokens/month depending on model choice and quantization. but hosted gives you elasticity and no infra ops. we usually recommend a pilot: run hosted with aggressive batching/caching configuration and measure, then evaluate a dedicated baseline for peak/steady.
[02:05] Elena: what's the overhead to set up dedicated?
[02:08] Maya: there's a contractual commit (monthly/annual) and minor integration work — you can keep same API surface. Redwood Dedicated provides reserved GPU pools, autoscaling policies and burst options so you don't have to manage infra. on private deployments, you get a customer control plane and can do on-prem for regulated data, but that has higher setup & maintenance.
[02:28] Priya: we will likely need a VPC option for certain datasets. also SSO and SOC2 are must-haves.
[02:33] Maya: we have SOC2, SAML/SSO, RBAC, KMS integrations — we'll send security pack.
[02:38] Jon: on batching — our requests are interactive single-turn prompts often with embeddings and RAG. how much batching can we realistically do without hurting latency?
[02:45] Ravi: continuous batching helps — we can batch small windows (10-50ms) to group requests without hurting median latency much. for interactive apps you usually see 5-20% latency increase for large batches but 30-60% cost reduction on per-token basis depending on kernel efficiency. also prefix/KV caching reduces repeated encoder cost for common retrieval contexts.
[03:06] Elena: KV cache — we've heard that term, is that the same thing as prefix caching?
[03:09] Ravi: yes, sometimes folks call it prefix or KV cache; it's storing key/value attention cache between requests so tokens from the retrieved context aren't recomputed. for RAG it's huge because your retrieved context repeats across queries for the same doc.
[03:22] Maya: we should also highlight model selection — smaller or quantized models reduce cost but quality tradeoffs vary. Redwood Optimize suggests quantization + model variant recommendations per workload.
[03:35] Priya: any numbers on int8 vs int4 in production?
[03:38] Ravi: int8 is fairly safe on many open models with minor quality impact; int4 can be great but requires evals. cost-wise int8 often cuts GPU memory & increases throughput, translating to 20-50% lower per-token compute cost; int4 can push that further but needs validation.
[03:55] Jon: what about cold-start and tail latency?
[03:57] Ravi: tail latency depends on batching policies, kernel selection and routing. Dedicated can guarantee latency SLOs better because you're not contending with other tenants; hosted has multi-tenant optimizations and transparent performance profiles. we'll share benchmark data.
[04:12] Elena: ok what's included in the cost model you send?
[04:15] Maya: we'll include hosted per-token price matrix by model size, a dedicated amortized cost example for a 4xA100 pool, suggested batching windows, caching hit assumptions, and expected per-token math for your traffic profile.
[04:26] Priya: do you support streaming outputs and how does that affect cost?
[04:29] Ravi: yes streaming is supported; cost is still per-token but streaming can improve perceived latency for users. for batching streaming, you typically do per-token billing on generated tokens and network overhead is minor.
[04:39] Jon: a practical question: our team has a $15k/mo constraint for procurement. what's the minimum we can pilot with?
[04:44] Maya: pilot can be done on hosted for as little as a few thousand dollars; we often run a 30-day pilot with a scoped dataset and traffic replay to estimate savings. if the pilot proves out, we can model a dedicated commit that meets your cost target.
[04:58] Elena: we'll want clear success metrics — cost per effective query, median and 95th latency, and percent of queries served from cache.
[05:05] Ravi: agreed. add quality metrics like exact-match/ROUGE for retrieval aug gen where applicable.

[05:12] -- Technical deep dive portion (Ravi leads) --
[05:15] [05:15] Ravi: can you share your prompt lengths and typical context size?
[05:18] Jon: prompts average 250 tokens, retrieved context another 700 tokens, typical completion 120 tokens.
[05:24] Ravi: ok so you're 1k-ish token roundtrip. that helps determine batching and memory footprint. with KV caching if many queries touch the same doc, you avoid recomputing the 700 token context. if cache hit rate is 30-50% your effective compute tokens drop a lot.
[05:38] Elena: our hit rate right now is low, but we can change retrieval strategy to increase it.
[05:42] Ravi: good — we'll include recommended retrieval tweaks in the checklist.

[06:00] -- Pricing examples discussion --
[06:05] Ravi: hypothetical: hosted per 1k tokens generative for M-model 13B = $0.20 per 1k (example). with batching and 30% cache hit you might drop effective cost to $0.14 per 1k. Dedicated amortized might be equivalent to $0.05-0.08 per 1k depending on utilization and instance type. these are illustrative - we'll put precise numbers in the spreadsheet.
[06:29] Priya: makes sense. the gap is big enough to pilot dedicated if utilization lines up. question: can dedicated burst to hosted?
[06:36] Maya: yes, Redwood supports mixed routing — you can route overflow to hosted to handle spikes so you don't have to overcommit.
[06:42] Jon: that sounds ideal because our usage is bursty.

[07:00] -- Security & compliance --
[07:05] Priya: we need SOC2 docs, KMS integration, SAML and audit logs. also data residency for certain data sets.
[07:12] Maya: we'll send the security pack and a sample SOC2 report. for private, we can do VPC + customer-managed KMS.

[07:22] -- Pilot scope & next steps recap --
[07:25] Maya: proposed pilot: 30 days, hosted with focused dataset, replay 2 weeks of traffic, measure cache hit, latency, and cost delta after enabling batching/cache/quantization. deliverables: benchmark report + recommendation for dedicated sizing.
[07:40] Elena: sounds good. timeline: we can share data by next Wed.
[07:43] Maya: action items — we'll follow up with the pricing spreadsheet, benchmark checklist and security docs.
[07:50] Priya: one more Q: competitor comparison, you mentioned Replicate and Bedrock — how do you position vs them?
[07:55] Maya: Replicate is more self-hosted model hosting marketplace; Bedrock is broad ML infra with big cloud lock-in. Redwood focuses on production serving, observability, cost levers and deployment flexibility (hosted/dedicated/private) and first-class tooling for rollouts and evaluations.
[08:10] Jon: ok thanks.

[08:15] -- End of recorded portion; remaining minutes were clarifying logistics and confirming dates. --

Recap and explicit next steps at close:
- Maya to send pricing & cost model spreadsheet (hosted vs dedicated examples) and security pack by 2026-03-23.
- Ravi to send benchmark checklist and recommended prompt/test set by 2026-03-24.
- Customer (Elena) to share current monthly token counts and a small sample dataset by 2026-03-25 to enable pilot planning.

Notes about transcription quality: some technical terms (KV cache, quantization) occasionally transcribed as K V cache or quantize, and names may be slightly off.
